newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister sees budget, not economic, crisis.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister sees budget, not economic, crisis.

text.p: MOSCOW, April 18 - Russia's decision to dump its 1997 plans and cut spending across the board to ease a budget crisis will not rebound badly on the rest of the economy, reform chief Anatoly Chubais said on Friday.

Chubais, also finance minister and one of two first deputy prime ministers, said a plan to sequester spending in the 1997 budget -- cutting spending across the board -- would leave second half spending little changed from that in the first half.
"The budget crisis is not a crisis for the country as a whole. It is not even a crisis for the whole economy," Chubais told a news conference.

"Budget recipients will get not less but more in the third and fourth quarters than they got in the first half of the year," he said. "This sequestration is about the truth...that the government will say what it can do and do it."

The Russian economy grew very slightly in the first quarter, after shrinking six percent in 1996, although government statisticians say this year's figures give the unreported shadow economy a better representation.
Chubais said the finance ministry would outline its new spending plans to the government next week.
Jochen Wermuth, head of the ministry's Economic Expert Group said this year would be no worse than the last from the point of view of government expenditure, even after sequestration.

"If you compare spending to the planned budget, then lots of things get cut. If you compare it to de facto 1996, it will be very similar, in the sense that all protected items will be covered and others will get two percent less of GDP," he said.
The Russian budget includes so-called protected items like health, education and the military where spending cannot be cut.

But low tax revenues mean it has to be revised. Chubais, the architect of Russian privatisation, told the conservative State Duma lower house of parliament on Thursday that first quarter tax collection was running at just 39 percent of target.
Deputies have already indicated that sequestration plans -- effectively a new budget -- will face a rough ride in the Duma, which stalled the passage of the original budget for months.
Chubais also promised to crack down on tax collection and two major tax debtors said they would issue securities to be transferred to the government as part of a plan to pay arrears.

Yukos oil company, one of the largest oil companies in the world by reserves, plans to issue debt and Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's largest metals producers, said its main unit would issue new shares.
The government would hold the securities during the repayment period and, according to a recent plan, could sell them if the companies fall behind in payments.
Chubais dismissed fears of capital flight, which a number of Western economists have said is still a problem for Russia.
"There is no problem with capital flight," he said. "That was a problem in 1993 and 1994 when the rouble fell three or four percent per day."

But Deutsche Morgan Grenfell estimated that Russian companies and individuals sent $20-$30 billion abroad for safe keeping in 1996 against $2.2 billion direct foreign investment and $8.0 billion for foreign portfolio and T-bill investment.
"The problem is not capital flight but collecting taxes on capital that is being taken out," Chubais said.
